senses.gloss: Simple and ordinary, not sophisticated.
examples: My grandfather was full of *homespun* wisdom.
The mayor's style is friendly and *homespun*.
Her second novel is more *homespun* than the first.

senses.gloss: Of cloth: spun or woven at home.
examples: The museum displays *homespun* shirts from the 1800s.
Pioneer families wore rough *homespun* cloth.

contrast: In American English *homey* means cozy, but *homely* means plain or unattractive: *a homey kitchen*, *a homely face*. In British English *homely* means cozy. Do not confuse either with the slang noun *homie* (a friend).

senses.gloss: Comfortable and pleasant, like being at home.
examples: The restaurant has a warm, *homey* feel.
They made the small apartment look *homey*.
With the rug and the lamps, the room felt much *homier*.

senses.gloss: Likely to kill someone, or wanting to kill.
senses.ru: склонный к убийству, одержимый жаждой убийства
examples: The movie is about a *homicidal* maniac in a small town.
Doctors said the patient had *homicidal* thoughts.
He became *homicidal* when he stopped taking his medication.

form: -ing from *home* (verb: to find the way home or to a target)

senses.gloss: Able to find its way home, or guided toward a target.
examples: *Homing* pigeons can fly hundreds of miles back to their loft.
The missile has a heat-seeking *homing* system.
Salmon have a strong *homing* instinct.

contrast: The variant *homogenous* (huh-MAH-juh-nuhs) is very common in American speech and writing with the same meaning.

senses.gloss: Made of parts or people that are all the same kind.
examples: The town's population was fairly *homogeneous*.
Stir the mixture until it is *homogeneous*.
Suburbs are often more *homogeneous* than big cities.

comparison: not gradable — but *more homogenized* in the 'too uniform' sense

senses.gloss: Of milk: treated so that the cream is mixed in and does not separate.
examples: Most milk sold in stores is *homogenized*.
She buys *homogenized* whole milk for the kids.

senses.gloss: Made so similar that it has lost variety or character.
examples: Critics complain about *homogenized* pop music.
Every mall now looks the same — American shopping has become more *homogenized*.

senses.gloss: Showing fear or hatred of gay people.
examples: The player was suspended for a *homophobic* slur.
Some of his old jokes now seem *homophobic*.
Attitudes in the town were more *homophobic* twenty years ago.

contrast: In everyday American English *gay* is the normal word; *homosexual* sounds clinical, and the noun *a homosexual* can sound offensive.

senses.gloss: Sexually attracted to people of the same sex.
examples: The study surveyed both *homosexual* and heterosexual couples.
*Homosexual* relationships were illegal in many states until 2003.
He told his family that he was *homosexual*.

contrast: Always a capital letter. *a Honduran* is a noun (a person from Honduras).

senses.gloss: From or relating to Honduras.
examples: We ate at a *Honduran* restaurant in Houston.
Her parents are *Honduran*.
*Honduran* coffee is exported all over the world.

contrast: The *h* is silent, so it is *an honest man*, not *a honest man*.

senses.gloss: Telling the truth and not cheating or stealing.
examples: He's an *honest* mechanic who never overcharges.
The cashier was *honest* and gave back the extra money.
She's the most *honest* person I know.

senses.gloss: Saying what you really think; frank.
examples: Be *honest* with me — do you like it?
To be *honest*, I'm not sure it will work.
Can I get your *honest* opinion about the draft?

senses.gloss: Of work or a mistake: fair, done without bad intentions.
examples: It was an *honest* mistake — he didn't mean to take your seat.
They made an *honest* living running a farm.

form: compound — from the oath *honest to God*
contrast: Often written *honest-to-God*; informal. After a verb *honest to God* is an exclamation (*Honest to God, I didn't know*), not an adjective. The milder form is *honest-to-goodness*.

senses.gloss: Real and genuine, used for emphasis.
examples: He's an *honest-to-God* hero.
It was the first *honest-to-god* snowstorm of the year.
We finally had an *honest-to-God* conversation about money.

form: compound — from the phrase *honest to goodness*

senses.gloss: Real and genuine, used for emphasis; informal.
examples: They served *honest-to-goodness* Southern barbecue.
She's an *honest-to-goodness* rocket scientist.
It was an *honest-to-goodness* miracle that nobody got hurt.

senses.gloss: Golden brown, like the color of honey.
examples: She had long, *honey-colored* hair.
The wooden floors were *honey-colored* and shiny.
The puppy looked up at us with *honey-colored* eyes.

contrast: Do not confuse with *honorary* (an honorary degree — given as an honor). *The Honorable* is also a title for judges and officials. British spelling is *honourable*.

senses.gloss: Honest, fair and deserving respect.
examples: He did the *honorable* thing and resigned.
Her intentions were completely *honorable*.
Admitting the mistake would have been more *honorable* than hiding it.

senses.gloss: Given with honor, not with disgrace.
examples: He received an *honorable* discharge from the Army.
Our school's film got an *honorable* mention at the festival.

contrast: *honorary* means given as an honor; *honorable* means morally good: *an honorary member*, *an honorable man*.

senses.gloss: Given as an honor, without the usual requirements or duties.
examples: The actor received an *honorary* degree from Yale.
They made her an *honorary* citizen of the city.
He's the *honorary* chairman, so he doesn't get paid.

senses.gloss: Proud and pleased because you have been shown respect.
examples: I'm *honored* to be here tonight.
We were *honored* by the invitation.
I've never felt more *honored* in my life.

senses.gloss: Respected and treated with special attention.
examples: The veterans were the *honored* guests at the parade.
Grandma had the *honored* place at the head of the table.

position: both — *a hooked nose*, but *hooked on* only after a verb

senses.gloss: Liking something so much that you cannot stop; addicted.
examples: I watched one episode and now I'm *hooked*.
He got *hooked* on painkillers after the surgery.
The more she played, the more *hooked* she got.

senses.gloss: Curved like a hook.
examples: The old man had a long, *hooked* nose.
Eagles have sharp, *hooked* beaks.

senses.gloss: Wanted and expected.
examples: The new policy didn't bring the *hoped-for* results.
The *hoped-for* rain finally arrived in August.
Sales never reached the *hoped-for* level.

senses.gloss: Believing that something good will happen.
examples: The doctors are *hopeful* that she'll make a full recovery.
We're *hopeful* about the new coach.
I feel more *hopeful* than I did last week.

senses.gloss: Making you think that something good will happen.
examples: The latest numbers are a *hopeful* sign.
The talks ended on a *hopeful* note.

senses.gloss: Flat and level, parallel to the ground.
examples: Draw a *horizontal* line across the page.
The flag has three *horizontal* stripes.
Make sure the shelf is perfectly *horizontal*.

senses.gloss: Relating to hormones.
examples: Acne is often caused by *hormonal* changes.
She was prescribed *hormonal* birth control.

senses.gloss: Informal: moody or emotional because of changes in hormones.
examples: Our fourteen-year-old is really *hormonal* right now.
Sorry I snapped at you — I'm just *hormonal* today.

senses.gloss: Of glasses: with thick frames made of horn or plastic that looks like horn.
examples: The professor wore *horn-rimmed* glasses.
He took off his *horn-rimmed* spectacles and rubbed his eyes.
Her new frames are black and *horn-rimmed*.

senses.gloss: Having horns or parts that look like horns.
examples: We saw a great *horned* owl in the barn.
The Vikings in the cartoon wore *horned* helmets.
*Horned* lizards live in the deserts of the Southwest.

contrast: The 'sexually excited' meaning is by far the most common, so the word sounds crude in polite conversation even when you mean the hard, horn-like sense.

senses.gloss: Informal: feeling sexual desire.
examples: The movie is about a bunch of *horny* teenagers at summer camp.
He joked that the spring weather made everyone *horny*.

senses.gloss: Hard and rough, like horn.
examples: Turtles have a *horny* beak instead of teeth.
The skin on his heels grew *hornier* every summer.

comparison: more/most — *more horrendous*, *most horrendous*; extreme, so *absolutely horrendous* rather than *very horrendous*

senses.gloss: Extremely bad or unpleasant.
examples: The traffic on the freeway was *horrendous*.
They paid a *horrendous* price for that house.
It was the most *horrendous* flight I've ever taken.

comparison: more/most — *more horrible*, *most horrible*; *really horrible* or *absolutely horrible* rather than *very horrible*

senses.gloss: Very bad, unpleasant or frightening.
examples: I had a *horrible* dream last night.
The coffee at the office tastes *horrible*.
That was the most *horrible* thing anyone has ever said to me.

senses.gloss: Unkind or mean to people.
examples: Why are you being so *horrible* to your sister?
She had a *horrible* boss at her first job.

contrast: *horrid* sounds a little old-fashioned or childish in American English; *horrible* is the everyday word.

senses.gloss: Very unpleasant or unkind.
examples: The medicine had a *horrid* taste.
Don't be so *horrid* to your little brother.
The second hotel was even more *horrid* than the first.

senses.gloss: Shocking and terrible, often because people are hurt or killed.
examples: Three people died in a *horrific* crash on the interstate.
The pictures from the war zone were *horrific*.
It was one of the most *horrific* crimes in the city's history.

contrast: *horrified* is how you feel; *horrifying* is what makes you feel that way: *We were horrified by the horrifying news*.

senses.gloss: Very shocked and upset.
examples: I was *horrified* to see how thin he had become.
Parents were *horrified* by the video.
She looked even more *horrified* when she saw the bill.

senses.gloss: Very shocking and frightening.
examples: The survivors told *horrifying* stories.
Watching the building collapse was *horrifying*.
The most *horrifying* part was not knowing where the kids were.

form: compound — noun + participle (*drawn by a horse*)

senses.gloss: Pulled by a horse or horses.
examples: We took a *horse-drawn* carriage ride through Central Park.
The Amish still travel in *horse-drawn* buggies.
In 1900 most delivery wagons in the city were *horse-drawn*.

senses.gloss: Relating to growing fruit, vegetables and flowers.
examples: She's studying *horticultural* science at Cornell.
The county fair has a big *horticultural* show.
The nursery sells *horticultural* supplies.

contrast: Also said HAHS-pi-tuh-buhl, with the stress on the first syllable.

senses.gloss: Friendly and generous to guests.
examples: Our hosts in Georgia were incredibly *hospitable*.
Southerners have a reputation for being *hospitable*.
The locals were far more *hospitable* than we expected.

senses.gloss: Of a place or conditions: good for living or growing in.
examples: The warm, wet soil is *hospitable* to many plants.
Mars is not a *hospitable* place for humans.

contrast: American English says HAHS-tuhl; British English says HOS-tyl.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly and ready to argue or fight.
examples: The crowd was *hostile* toward the speaker.
He gave me a *hostile* look.
Voters have grown more *hostile* to new taxes.

senses.gloss: Belonging to an enemy in a war.
examples: The pilots flew deep into *hostile* territory.
Radar picked up two *hostile* aircraft.

senses.gloss: Of conditions: difficult and dangerous to live or work in.
examples: The Arctic is one of the most *hostile* environments on Earth.
Many women described a *hostile* work environment.

position: predicative only — usually after *get* or *be*, often with *all*
comparison: not gradable — intensified with *all*: *all hot and bothered*

senses.gloss: Upset, worried or angry about something, often more than necessary.
examples: Don't get all *hot and bothered* over a parking ticket.
The fans got *hot and bothered* about the referee's call.
She was *hot and bothered* after waiting an hour for the bus.

senses.gloss: Informal: sexually excited.
examples: The love scene got the audience all *hot and bothered*.
He was clearly *hot and bothered* when she walked in.

senses.gloss: Angry or annoyed; informal.
examples: Dad gets *hot under the collar* when people cut in line.
The senator was clearly *hot under the collar* about the question.
Calm down — there's no reason to get *hot under the collar*.

senses.gloss: Passionate and quick to get angry or excited.
examples: He was a *hot-blooded* young man who loved a fight.
The coach is famously *hot-blooded* on the sidelines.
Her brother was even more *hot-blooded* than she was.

senses.gloss: Getting angry very easily.
examples: My grandfather was a *hot-tempered* man.
The new chef is talented but *hot-tempered*.
She was the most *hot-tempered* player on the team.

senses.gloss: Acting too quickly, without thinking, often out of anger.
examples: A *hotheaded* driver started yelling at us.
He was *hotheaded* when he was young, but he's calmed down.
The younger brother was even more *hotheaded*.

senses.gloss: Lasting one hour.
examples: We had an *hourlong* meeting with the principal.
The show is an *hourlong* drama.
After an *hourlong* wait, we finally got a table.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is an adverb without hyphens: *go house to house*

senses.gloss: Going to every house in an area, one after another.
examples: Police did a *house-to-house* search for the missing boy.
Volunteers ran a *house-to-house* campaign before the election.
The census used to rely on *house-to-house* visits.

senses.gloss: Unable to leave home, usually because of illness or old age.
senses.ru: прикованный к дому, не выходящий из дома
examples: Since her hip surgery, she's been *housebound*.
Volunteers deliver meals to *housebound* seniors.
The blizzard kept us *housebound* for three days.

contrast: American English says *housebroken*; British English says *house-trained*.

senses.gloss: Of a pet: trained to go to the bathroom outside or in a box.
examples: Is the puppy *housebroken* yet?
The shelter only adopts out *housebroken* dogs.
It took us two months to get the dog fully *housebroken*.

senses.gloss: Of wind or a storm: blowing hard with a long, loud noise.
examples: We huddled in the tent while a *howling* wind shook it.
The ship sailed straight into a *howling* storm.

senses.gloss: Informal: very great, used for emphasis.
examples: The play was a *howling* success.
Leaving the keys in the car was a *howling* mistake.

senses.gloss: Crowded close together, or curled up, especially for warmth or safety.
examples: The kids were *huddled* around the campfire.
We found the cat *huddled* under the porch.
Reporters spoke to *huddled* groups of refugees at the border.

senses.gloss: Annoyed and easily offended, and showing it.
examples: He got *huffy* when I asked him to turn the music down.
She sent me a *huffy* email about the schedule.
The *huffier* he gets, the less anyone listens.

form: -ing from *hulk* (a big, heavy person or thing)

senses.gloss: Very big and heavy, often in a clumsy or threatening way.
examples: A *hulking* bouncer stood at the door.
The *hulking* old factory has been empty for years.
He's a *hulking* offensive lineman who weighs 320 pounds.

comparison: not gradable — but *more human* in the 'showing feelings and weaknesses' sense
contrast: *human* means of people; *humane* means kind and not cruel: *human rights*, *humane treatment*. *a human* is also a noun.

senses.gloss: Of or relating to people.
examples: The *human* body has 206 bones.
The accident was caused by *human* error.
Dogs can hear sounds that *human* ears cannot.

senses.gloss: Having the normal feelings and weaknesses that people have.
examples: Don't be so hard on yourself — you're only *human*.
The interview showed a more *human* side of the senator.
It's *human* to make mistakes.

contrast: American spelling is *centered*; British English writes *centred*.

senses.gloss: Designed around the needs and experience of the people who will use it.
examples: The company takes a *human-centered* approach to design.
Good health care should be *human-centered*.
The new app is far more *human-centered* than the old one.

contrast: *humane* (hyoo-MAYN) means kind; *human* (HYOO-muhn) means of people. The stress moves.

senses.gloss: Kind to people and animals, and not causing unnecessary suffering.
examples: The shelter uses *humane* traps to catch stray cats.
Prisoners must be treated in a *humane* way.
There has to be a more *humane* solution.

contrast: *a humanist* is also a noun (a person). *humanistic* is the adjective that can follow a verb: *His approach is humanistic*.

senses.gloss: Relating to humanism, a way of thinking that values human reason and needs rather than religion.
examples: The group holds *humanist* wedding ceremonies.
Renaissance *humanist* scholars studied Greek and Latin texts.
She was raised with *humanist* values.

senses.gloss: Focused on human values, needs and potential.
examples: The school takes a *humanistic* approach to education.
Carl Rogers founded *humanistic* psychology.
Her philosophy of medicine is deeply *humanistic*.

contrast: False friend: *humanitarian* is about helping people who suffer (*humanitarian aid*), not about the arts and literature. Russian *гуманитарные науки* is *the humanities*.

senses.gloss: Helping people who are suffering, especially after a war or disaster.
examples: The UN sent *humanitarian* aid to the region.
Doctors called it a *humanitarian* crisis.
The decision to reopen the border was *humanitarian*, not political.

contrast: *humbled* is how you feel; *humbling* is what makes you feel it: *a humbling experience left me humbled*.

senses.gloss: Feeling less proud or important, often because of someone's kindness or praise.
examples: I'm *humbled* by all your support.
She said she was *humbled* to receive the award.
After losing 7–0, the team looked *humbled*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel less proud or important.
examples: Losing in the first round was a *humbling* experience.
Working with such talented people is *humbling*.
It was the most *humbling* moment of my career.

senses.gloss: Boring and ordinary, with nothing new or exciting.
examples: He wanted to escape his *humdrum* office job.
Life in a small town can feel *humdrum*.
The sequel was even more *humdrum* than the original.

contrast: *humid* is used for air and weather; for a damp towel or wet ground say *damp* or *wet*.

senses.gloss: Of air or weather: warm and full of moisture.
examples: Summers in Houston are hot and *humid*.
It's a *humid* day, so the laundry won't dry.
Florida is more *humid* than Arizona.

contrast: *humiliated* is how you feel; *humiliating* is what makes you feel that way: *a humiliating defeat*, *a humiliated team*.

senses.gloss: Feeling ashamed and foolish in front of other people.
examples: I felt *humiliated* when the teacher read my note to the class.
The *humiliated* champion left the ring without a word.
I've never been more *humiliated* in my life.

senses.gloss: Making you feel ashamed and foolish.
examples: The team suffered a *humiliating* defeat.
Having to ask my parents for money was *humiliating*.
It was the most *humiliating* day of my life.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *absolutely humongous*, not *very humongous*
contrast: Informal and a little playful; use *huge* or *enormous* in formal writing.

senses.gloss: Informal: extremely big.
examples: They live in a *humongous* house on the lake.
The portions at that diner are *humongous*.
He ordered a *humongous* plate of nachos.

contrast: American spelling is *humorless*; British English writes *humourless*.

senses.gloss: Having no sense of humor; too serious.
examples: The new manager is strict and *humorless*.
She gave a *humorless* laugh.
He's the most *humorless* person I've ever worked with.

contrast: Spelled *humorous* in both American and British English, even though British *humour* has a *u*.

senses.gloss: Funny and entertaining.
examples: He gave a *humorous* speech at the wedding.
Her column is smart and *humorous*.
The second half of the book is more *humorous* than the first.

senses.gloss: With the back and shoulders bent forward.
examples: He sat *hunched* over his laptop all day.
She walked with *hunched* shoulders against the cold.
An old man sat *hunched* on the bench.

contrast: Always a capital letter. *a Hungarian* is a person and *Hungarian* is the language — both nouns.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Hungary, its people or its language.
examples: She makes a great *Hungarian* goulash.
My grandparents were *Hungarian*.
*Hungarian* grammar is famously difficult.

contrast: Informal and a little old-fashioned; often used ironically: *Everything's not exactly hunky-dory*.

senses.gloss: Informal: fine, with no problems.
examples: Everything is *hunky-dory* at home.
He acts like everything's *hunky-dory*, but he's worried.
The deal looked *hunky-dory* until the lawyers read it.

senses.gloss: Looking frightened and worried, as if someone is chasing you.
examples: He had a *hunted* look in his eyes.
After weeks on the run, she looked thin and *hunted*.

senses.gloss: Being searched for or chased in order to be caught or killed.
examples: After the escape he was a *hunted* man.
Wolves were once the most *hunted* animals in the state.

senses.gloss: Done quickly because there is not much time.
examples: We ate a *hurried* breakfast and ran for the bus.
His goodbye was short and *hurried*.
The second draft felt more *hurried* than the first.

form: past participle of *hurt* — the same form as the verb
contrast: The past participle is *hurt*, never *hurted*. For a serious wound, *injured* or *wounded* is more exact.

senses.gloss: Injured, with pain in part of the body.
examples: Are you *hurt*? Can you stand up?
Two players were badly *hurt* in the collision.
The *hurt* hiker was carried down the trail.

senses.gloss: Upset and offended by what someone said or did.
examples: She was *hurt* that nobody remembered her birthday.
I tried not to show my *hurt* feelings.
He was more *hurt* by her silence than by her words.

senses.gloss: Making someone feel upset or offended.
examples: That was a really *hurtful* thing to say.
His comments about her weight were *hurtful*.
Being ignored was more *hurtful* than being criticized.

senses.gloss: Informal: kept secret.
examples: The project is all very *hush-hush*.
They held a *hush-hush* meeting with the investors.
The wedding plans were even more *hush-hush* than the engagement.

senses.gloss: Very quiet, or spoken quietly.
examples: They spoke in *hushed* voices so they wouldn't wake the baby.
The courtroom was *hushed* as the verdict was read.
A *hushed* crowd watched the final putt.

contrast: *a husky* is also a noun — a sled dog. In US stores, *husky* sizes are clothes for heavier boys.

senses.gloss: Of a voice: low and slightly rough.
examples: She has a warm, *husky* voice.
His voice was *husky* from shouting at the game.
Her voice got *huskier* as the night went on.

senses.gloss: Of a person: big, strong and heavy.
examples: A *husky* young farmhand lifted the bales.
He was a *husky* kid who grew into a football player.

contrast: *a hybrid* is also a noun: *She drives a hybrid*.

senses.gloss: Made by combining two different kinds of things.
examples: We bought a *hybrid* car to save on gas.
The company switched to a *hybrid* work model — three days in the office, two at home.
The tomato plants in the garden are *hybrid*.

senses.gloss: Having enough water in the body or skin.
senses.ru: с достаточным количеством воды в организме; увлажнённый
examples: Drink plenty of water to stay *hydrated* in the heat.
This lotion keeps your skin *hydrated*.
I feel more *hydrated* since I started carrying a water bottle.

senses.gloss: Moved or operated by the pressure of water or oil.
examples: The truck has a *hydraulic* lift.
The mechanic found a leak in the *hydraulic* brakes.
*Hydraulic* fracturing is used to get oil and gas out of rock.

senses.gloss: Producing electricity from the force of moving water.
examples: Hoover Dam is a huge *hydroelectric* plant.
The state gets most of its power from *hydroelectric* dams.
*Hydroelectric* energy is cheap in the Pacific Northwest.

senses.gloss: Growing plants in water with nutrients, without soil.
examples: They grow lettuce in a *hydroponic* greenhouse.
The restaurant has its own *hydroponic* herb garden.
*Hydroponic* farms use much less water than ordinary fields.

senses.gloss: Clean and not likely to spread disease.
examples: The kitchen didn't look very *hygienic*.
Nurses wear gloves for *hygienic* reasons.
Paper towels are more *hygienic* than hand dryers.

senses.gloss: Too active, and unable to stay still or focus.
examples: Sugar makes my kids *hyperactive*.
He was diagnosed as a *hyperactive* child.
The puppy is even more *hyperactive* after a nap.

senses.gloss: Exaggerated; saying something is much bigger or worse than it is.
examples: Calling it 'the worst day in history' is a little *hyperbolic*.
The ad made *hyperbolic* claims about the product.
The headlines got more *hyperbolic* every day.

senses.gloss: In math: relating to a hyperbola.
examples: We studied *hyperbolic* functions in calculus.
The comet followed a *hyperbolic* path.

senses.gloss: Too easily affected, upset or offended.
examples: Some people are *hypersensitive* to noise.
He's *hypersensitive* about his height.
Her skin became even more *hypersensitive* after the treatment.

senses.gloss: Holding your attention in a way that makes you feel calm or sleepy.
examples: The song has a slow, *hypnotic* beat.
Watching the waves was almost *hypnotic*.
Her voice was even more *hypnotic* in person.

senses.gloss: Relating to hypnosis.
examples: The patient was put into a *hypnotic* trance.
Some therapists use *hypnotic* techniques to treat anxiety.

contrast: American spelling is *hypnotized*; British English also writes *hypnotised*.

senses.gloss: So interested in something that you cannot look away.
examples: The kids sat *hypnotized* by the cartoon.
I was *hypnotized* by the northern lights.

senses.gloss: Put into a state of hypnosis.
examples: The *hypnotized* volunteer started clucking like a chicken.
She claims she quit smoking after being *hypnotized*.

takes: *of* + person + *to*-infinitive: *It's hypocritical of him to complain*

senses.gloss: Saying you believe one thing but doing the opposite.
examples: It's *hypocritical* of him to lecture us about saving money.
Voters were angry at the *hypocritical* senator.
Nothing is more *hypocritical* than preaching honesty and then lying.

senses.gloss: Used to inject drugs under the skin.
examples: The nurse filled a *hypodermic* syringe.
Kids found a used *hypodermic* needle in the park.
The vaccine was given by *hypodermic* injection.

senses.gloss: Imagined as possible, but not real or not yet true.
examples: Let me ask you a *hypothetical* question.
The danger is not just *hypothetical* — it has happened before.
The lawyers argued about a *hypothetical* situation.

contrast: In informal American English *hysterical* very often means *very funny*: *That video is hysterical!*

senses.gloss: Out of control because of strong emotion, such as fear or grief.
examples: The mother became *hysterical* when she couldn't find her son.
Stop being *hysterical* and listen to me.
The crowd grew more *hysterical* as the fire spread.

senses.gloss: Informal: extremely funny.
examples: Her impression of the boss was *hysterical*.
It's the most *hysterical* movie I've seen all year.

senses.gloss: Relating to Spain and Portugal, or the peninsula they share.
examples: Spain and Portugal make up the *Iberian* Peninsula.
The restaurant serves *Iberian* ham and cheese.
The architecture of the old mission is clearly *Iberian*.

contrast: Always a capital letter. The language is *Icelandic* (noun); a person is *an Icelander*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Iceland, its people or its language.
examples: We tried *Icelandic* yogurt on our trip.
The band is *Icelandic*.
*Icelandic* horses are small but very strong.

comparison: not gradable — extreme: *already ice-cold*, not *very ice-cold*

senses.gloss: Extremely cold.
examples: Nothing beats an *ice-cold* lemonade in July.
The water in the lake was *ice-cold*.
My hands were *ice-cold* after shoveling snow.

senses.gloss: Showing no emotion or friendliness; calm under pressure.
examples: She gave him an *ice-cold* stare.
The kicker was *ice-cold* in the final seconds.

contrast: Informal and childish-sounding; adults use it for mild disgust or discomfort.

senses.gloss: Informal: unpleasant, sticky or disgusting.
examples: There's something *icky* on the bottom of my shoe.
The whole situation made me feel *icky*.
That was the *ickiest* bathroom I've ever seen.

contrast: Not *иконный*: *iconic* means very famous and seen as a symbol of something.

senses.gloss: Very famous and seen as a symbol of a time, place or idea.
examples: The Golden Gate Bridge is an *iconic* landmark.
Her red dress in the film became *iconic*.
It's one of the most *iconic* photos of the twentieth century.

form: -ic from *iconoclast* (a person who attacks accepted beliefs)

senses.gloss: Attacking or rejecting accepted beliefs and traditions.
examples: He was an *iconoclastic* filmmaker who broke every rule.
Her ideas about economics were considered *iconoclastic*.
The band's second album was even more *iconoclastic*.

senses.gloss: Covered with ice.
examples: Drive slowly — the roads are *icy*.
She slipped on the *icy* sidewalk.

senses.gloss: Extremely cold.
examples: An *icy* wind blew off the lake.
January is the *iciest* month in Chicago.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly and showing no warm feelings.
examples: He gave me an *icy* stare.
Her voice was polite but *icy*.

comparison: not gradable — already means 'the best'; *more ideal* is heard in speech but avoided in careful writing
contrast: *an ideal* is also a noun (a principle). *In an ideal world* means 'if things were perfect', which they are not.

senses.gloss: Perfect, or the best possible for a purpose.
examples: This park is *ideal* for a picnic.
She's the *ideal* candidate for the job.
The weather was *ideal* for sailing.

senses.gloss: Existing only in the imagination, not in reality.
examples: In an *ideal* world, nobody would go hungry.
The *ideal* family on TV has nothing to do with real life.

senses.gloss: Believing that very good things are possible, often without being practical.
examples: She was a young, *idealistic* teacher who wanted to change the world.
His plan is *idealistic*, but it will never work.
I was more *idealistic* in college.

senses.gloss: Shown or imagined as better than it really is.
examples: The movie paints an *idealized* picture of small-town life.
Her memories of childhood are a little *idealized*.
Ads show a more *idealized* version of motherhood than real life does.

senses.gloss: Exactly the same.
examples: Mark and Mike are *identical* twins.
Your answer is *identical* to the one in the book.
The two houses look almost *identical*.

senses.gloss: Able to be recognized or named.
examples: The paramedics were easily *identifiable* by their uniforms.
The report removed all *identifiable* information about patients.
The newer logo is more *identifiable* from a distance.

senses.gloss: Based on a set of political or social beliefs.
examples: The two parties have deep *ideological* differences.
The Cold War was an *ideological* struggle.
His objections were *ideological*, not practical.
